# Applications: Mind, Body, Machine, The Role of AI/ML in the Future of Sports (SSAC23)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Draft routine documents with an LLM, then check every line. Morey described using a language model to produce a first draft that he edits in a few places [02:35, 03:05]. Applied Performance has named documentation gaps (sport-specific data dictionaries, daily checklists). A first draft of one could come from vendor documentation pasted in, with staff review. The panel's own warning is that the model can state wrong sports facts confidently [08:42, 09:43].
- Inference: Many correlated force plate metrics need a plan, not a rule of thumb. Morey said that with proper regularization, correlated variables and even more parameters than observations can be handled, while pure noise variables still make things worse and an analyst should still choose the inputs [12:15, 12:47, 13:49, 14:20]. This bears on how many VALD metrics go into any model of readiness or return to play.
- Inference: Keep readiness and risk flags explainable. Morey said there will always be a tension between explainability and predictive power [45:01], and a coach or owner who asks why gets a poor answer from a model that only says it is so [45:31]. Flags passed to coaches and Athletic Medicine should state the metric, the change and the comparison.
- Inference: Write a data policy before adding any new monitoring. Liao raised the question of what happens if a team requires athletes to wear devices that track sleep, glucose or more around the clock [31:42, 32:13]. Before Applied Performance adds a sleep or biometric stream, a consent and use rule should exist.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Metric selection uses 1 to 2 output metrics, 1 to 3 driver metrics, 1 to 3 strategy metrics, optional symmetry, and "fluffy" metrics only with a defensible rationale (Adopted practice, framework from Hawkin Dynamics). Morey's point that an analyst still curates inputs agrees.
- Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit). Liao's garbage-in, garbage-out point [16:23, 16:53] agrees.
- Eric's baseline: The current data dictionary is organized by vendor, not sport, and fixing that is a priority (Explicit). The LLM drafting idea would serve that task but the talk does not address it.
- Eric's baseline: Subjective daily wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them, but are kept for return-to-play and chronic conditions (Explicit). The talk's private-data discussion [29:38, 30:09] extends this: it argues that some factors (sleep, personal stress) cannot or should not be digitized, and that teams hold private data others do not.
- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (gap). The talk's AWS helmet-contact work [04:08] has no counterpart in his baseline.

## What would have to be true

- Written permission rules for what data may be pasted into any external language model. Per the DEV workspace handling note, identifiable health data is not pasted into external services.
- A named reviewer who checks any LLM-drafted procedure against the actual device and vendor manual.
- For any regularized model, enough athletes and observations to test out of sample. The panel did not state sample sizes, so that must be checked locally.

## Do not apply when

- The output affects an athlete's health or availability decision without a human reviewing it. Morey, Liao and others on the panel said the tools should assist, with humans in the loop [41:25, 49:38].
- The domain data are mostly not digitized. Panelists said that sleep, mood and personal context are not captured by public data [29:38].
- The claimed accuracy gain is applied to sports data. The 60% versus 80% figures Sherry Marcus gave were described as general science results, not sports [26:01, 26:32].
- Inference: The sample is a single college roster. Morey's draft-model remarks come from a professional organization with larger historical data [44:31, 47:05].

## First step

Inference: Choose one low-stakes Playbook gap (for example one vendor's metric definitions), draft it with an LLM using only vendor text you paste in, then verify each line against the vendor manual before it goes anywhere. Keep a note of what the model got wrong.

=== FILE: videos/2022-04-01_Q3i3FOC-dPE_using-tracking-and-charting-data-to-better-evaluate-nfl-play/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: Q3i3FOC-dPE
title: "SSAC22: Using Tracking and Charting Data to Better Evaluate NFL Players: A Review"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Eric Eager (introduced as being from Pro Football Focus)]
topics: [american-football, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Eager argues that football analytics has used its three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, and player tracking) mostly one at a time, and that combining them gives better player evaluation. He shows three cases from Pro Football Focus (PFF): an expected pressure rate for pass rushers, a "bite distance" measure for linebackers on play action, and a speed-adjusted receiver grade for deep routes. In each case the hand-charted grade supplies the target and tracking data supplies a measure that is steadier from year to year or tracks athletic testing. The Q&A covers second-order effects, trade-offs and model context.

## Key claims

- Football analytics has advanced from a few public writers to many data sources, but each source is mostly used alone, and combining them would improve player evaluation [01:33].
- PFF charts every NFL and college game by hand, producing player grades and event labels. The NFL's tracking data comes from chips in shoulder pads and the ball [02:08, 02:40].
- For pass rushers, PFF's charted pressure and win-rate data served as training targets, and tracking data supplied the predictors, in two models (pressure and win rate) [06:16].
- The most important predictor of a pressure was the defender's vertical distance covered in the first second. The model was an XGBoost ensemble of decision trees [06:47].
- Charted position labels (nose tackle, edge defender) also entered the model, so it carries some information on player type [07:18].
- Each play yields a pressure probability, not only a yes or no [07:48].
- Pressure is treated as the process that leads to sacks. PFF pressure rate and expected pressure rate together predict sack rate better than either alone, and tracking data also adds power when predicting a player's own pressure rate [08:19, 08:49].
- Expected pressure rate tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than charted data does, which gives a time-varying athleticism measure in place of one combine number [09:19, 09:50].
- Coverage grades are unstable year to year. Linebacker "bite distance under expected" (BDU), the vertical displacement on play action adjusted for situation, is more predictive year to year than the coverage grade [10:20, 11:22, 12:23].
- Eager's reasoning for BDU: biting on a fake leaves the middle of the field open, the most valuable area to throw [10:51, 11:22].
- A receiver model using mean, median and max speed over a play found speed to be the most important variable for a positive PFF grade on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55].
- The resulting speed-adjusted grade is steadier year to year than the deep-pass grade and correlates with the 40-yard dash, with exceptions such as Landry (slow 40, good receiver) and Kupp (faster on field than his timed run) [13:55, 14:25, 14:56].
- Tracking data's promise may not be reached without combining it with charting and play-by-play [15:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Sacks take about two points on average from an offense [05:45].
- Sack rate predicting itself year to year: about 0.24 (R squared), given with "I think" and "or something" [08:19].
- BDU is described as three or four times more predictive year to year (R squared) than the coverage grade. The captions read "about four times three or four times", so the exact multiple is garbled [11:53, 12:23].
- Kupp's pro-day 40 time: 4.62 (caption "cooper cup"; the speaker was unsure of the year and said 2017) [14:56].
- Pressure: charted when a rusher moves the quarterback off his spot or gets a sack. Win rate: charted as whether the rusher won the rep. The two are correlated but can differ [05:15, 05:45].
- PFF grades are discrete steps of half a point from negative two (caption wording) [26:36].
- First-second speed was measured in the vertical (y) direction and as straight-line distance [06:47].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Charted grades as labels, tracking features as predictors (pressure, win rate, receiver grade) [06:16, 13:25].
- XGBoost classification for pressure [06:47].
- Adjusting linebacker displacement for situation (run tendencies, down and distance) and averaging over time [11:22, 11:53].
- Year-to-year R squared as the test of whether a new measure is better than the existing grade [08:19, 12:23].

## Limits and open questions

- The slides are not visible. Most R squared values, sample sizes, seasons and the number of plays are not in the captions, so only the 0.24 and the "three or four times" claims can be quoted.
- The speaker works for PFF and presents PFF tools as results, so this is an institutional and commercial view.
- The 40-yard dash question (correlation of about 0.75 raised by a questioner) concerns career averages versus one-time combine results, not within-player prediction, and the exchange is partly unclear [22:31, 23:31].
- Eager agreed in Q&A that BDU says nothing alone about whether a defender's passivity is worth what it costs against the run [18:58, 19:28].
- The linebacker examples are individual cases (Warner, Kuechly, Hewitt, Cunningham, White, David as heard in the captions); no group-level validation is shown beyond the R squared claim [11:53, 18:58, 24:31].
- Names in the captions may be misspelled (Kuechly appears as "luke lee"; Okereke as "okariki").

## Q&A

- An economist-style questioner asked about second-order effects (tired linemen, scheme and play-calling changes). Eager agreed, noting football has many columns but few rows, and that the game changes quickly, with play action as an example [16:28, 16:58, 17:28].
- Is the linebacker metric the right objective, since it measures the mean rather than variance? Eager is studying the trade-off (a good run defender may accept some middle-field plays) and wants analytics to quantify it [18:28, 18:58, 19:28].
- Do the receiver rankings match popular opinion? Eager discussed Tyreek Hill and Antonio Brown (caption spelling "tyree kill") and argued the measure captures controlled speed usable for football plays [20:28, 20:59, 21:30].
- Clarifying the 40-yard R squared table: it uses careers, because players test only once [22:31, 23:01, 23:31].
- Do defensive backs or linebackers who cushion create bias? Eager suggested team-level view of the two inside linebackers, because one may bite while the other covers [24:01, 24:31, 25:02].
- Why do context variables such as yards to go matter in the grade model? PFF does not ask graders to do context math, and the model partly adjusts for it [26:03, 26:36, 27:07].

=== FILE: videos/2023-03-15_knZ8ImMzBX4_leveling-up-how-basketball-teams-deploy-analytics-to-develop/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: knZ8ImMzBX4
title: "SSAC23 - Leveling Up: How Basketball Teams Deploy Analytics to Develop Players"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Shane Battier, Catherine Evans (caption spelling), Mike sarin (caption spelling), Ben Cohen (moderator), Khalid McCaskill (introduction, caption spelling)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, sports-science]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel of a former NBA player turned executive, a Wizards research executive and a Celtics executive discusses how data supports player development. The panel agrees that game data is now similar across teams, so the edge lies in what teams do with it and in how it is communicated to players and coaches. It covers shot evaluation with context, the coming league pose data, staff composition, how players take in data, the gap between a player's skills and the role he is given, and the limits of basketball analogies to baseball biomechanics. Most of the content is opinion and anecdote, not shown analysis.

## Key claims

- Battier said that three things matter in basketball: making open shots, finishing, and drawing fouls. A Hall of Famer does all three, most All-Stars do two elite, and he would have focused on threes and finishing [02:36, 03:06, 03:36].
- Today's players know that shots at the rim are good but not why [04:38].
- Evans said three-point percentage is the best descriptive measure of what happened, but evaluating shooting ability needs shot quality, scheme, role and gym data, and contest level [06:11, 07:15].
- A "Splash Zone" ideal shot exists in theory, but different players have different effective shots, so context about who shoots matters [08:16, 08:46].
- Mike (Celtics) said the NBA's coming camera system adds body pose, which will help judge how contested a shot is, especially farther from the rim, and teams will build better shot models [10:47, 11:18].
- Zarren-type and Evans comments agree that in-game NBA data is largely the same across teams, and advantage comes from engineering and speed of use, not access [12:20, 12:53].
- Evans's ideal staff: data engineers, software engineers, a design person, ML and statistics PhDs, and former players who know some SQL and Python [13:54, 14:26].
- Mike said communication is as important as insight, and few people combine statistics, basketball knowledge and communication [15:26, 15:57]. Battier advised adding a behavioral psychology course and developing emotional intelligence [16:58].
- Battier said he persuaded LeBron James with a scouting note about one opponent's weaker side, and that players care that it works, not how the number was made [18:30, 19:01].
- Mike said players vary in interest in data, that small samples can mislead them, and the team wants one message across coaches and front office, so it leaves much communication to coaches [21:04, 21:34, 22:04].
- Evans said gym cameras give players immediate shot feedback, and younger players engage more [23:05, 23:35]. Panelists said data has become ordinary rather than players becoming more willing [24:36].
- Mike did not expect NBA players to buy their own data, since the team provides it, including a facility with force plates mounted separately to the ground [29:15, 29:47].
- Evans argued baseball-style biomechanics labs fit pitching more than basketball, because basketball involves constant decisions and defenders; free throws are the most mechanical case [31:18, 31:48, 32:19]. Another panelist countered that computer vision on phones will bring pose data [33:50].
- Panelists said players with more athleticism and opportunity can grow their games, and role players have less room to add skills [41:00, 41:32, 42:32]. Battier told his own move from power forward to guard as an example of opportunity [43:03].
- Evans framed development as separating who a player is from what he is asked to do, and looking for skills not used by his current team [44:36, 45:36, 46:06].
- Evans said she would pass practice-data drift to the coach and ask the medical staff whether compensation or injury explains it, rather than tell the player [46:37, 47:08].
- Battier said he would listen about his shot only to someone with long credibility, and recounted fixing his own shot before Game 7 [49:39, 50:10, 51:12].
- Evans said measuring decision quality is hard because the counterfactual is unobserved, and selection bias is strong [57:22, 57:53, 58:53].

## Numbers and definitions

- Three numbers per Battier: open shot (no-dribble jump shot), finishing at the rim, foul drawing [03:06, 03:36].
- Shooting "Splash Zone": about 45 degrees and 10 inches back, centered on the hoop (speaker's caption wording) [08:16].
- Current data: center of mass of each player about 30 times a second plus the ball. Coming system: 19 body points per player, mentioned at about 50 hertz [08:46, 09:16, 10:47].
- Battier's Durant example: "200 bips" better over one shoulder (caption wording, unclear); LeBron guarded him twice and Durant missed both [18:30]. Battier said he left out sample size and variance [19:01].
- The Celtics practiced as a full team about twice in January, with 82 games in the season [44:05].
- Half-court offense at 0.8 points per possession, from Battier's high school team, whose record the captions give as nine and fifteen [25:07, 25:38].
- The moderator's Lowry example gives a shot arc dropping from 46 or 47 degrees to 41 degrees; this is the moderator's retelling of a book, not a panelist's data [46:06].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Spatial tracking and shot-quality models, in-gym shooting data and contest-level adjustment [07:15].
- Synergy tags and video platform for players [21:04].
- Drill design as steps (on air, with a coach, practice game, game) with stated goals for each [34:53, 35:24].
- Counterfactual and expected-points reasoning for decisions, acknowledged as imperfect [57:53, 58:23, 58:53].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly opinion and personal anecdote; no model, data or sample is shown.
- Battier's Durant story rests on two possessions and he said he did not explain variance. He called the Kobe counter-analytics story unverifiable [18:30, 19:01, 27:11].
- Speakers are not labeled in the captions. Attribution above uses context (Celtics, Wizards and Battier's own history), and some lines, such as the free-throw volume argument and the comment that foul rate matters more than free-throw rate, cannot be assigned with certainty [36:25, 37:26].
- Each speaker speaks for an employer or personal experience, including claims that the team's data and facility make player-bought data unnecessary [29:47].
- Pose data accuracy was called uncertain by a panelist, and injury uses were left open [10:47, 11:18].
- Name and term problems in captions (Zarren as "sarin", Evans as "Katherine"/"Kathy", Khris Middleton as "Chris Middleton", "bips").

## Q&A

- Is development data focused too much on offense? Panelists disagreed with the premise and said defense, including team rotations, gets a lot of time [51:44, 52:15, 52:47].
- What do you wish you had live in games? Evans said not much; coaches recall plays well. Challenge decisions could use spatial data. The Celtics have a staffer behind the bench for challenges [53:47, 54:17, 54:47, 55:17, 55:49].
- Does a specific defender's closeout work analytically? The sample is small, and pose data is needed [56:21, 56:52].
- What data would you want that you lack? Decision-making measures; panelists discussed the counterfactual problem [57:22, 57:53, 58:23, 58:53].
- Final prompt: what the moderator will ask in 2039; load management was the joke answer [59:25].

=== FILE: videos/2023-03-15_tRnkF9eTWWg_mind-body-machine-the-role-of-ai-ml-in-the-future-of-sports/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: tRnkF9eTWWg
title: "SSAC23: Mind, Body, Machine: The Role of AI/ML in the Future of Sports"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Daryl Morey, Sherry Marcus, Patrick Lucy (caption spelling), Matthew Liao, Ethan Strauss (moderator), Nick Holmes (introduction)]
topics: [american-football, basketball, injury-health, policy, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel on AI and machine learning in sport with a basketball executive, an AWS AI director, a Stats Perform chief scientist and a bioethicist. The practical threads are large language models as productivity tools, new forecasting methods that tolerate many correlated predictors, fine-tuning a language model for NFL broadcast narratives, and health and safety applications. The cautionary threads are hallucination on sports facts, the black-box problem and the tension between explainability and predictive power, private versus public data, athlete monitoring and privacy, cheating, and whether humans stay in the loop. Panelists disagreed on how worried to be. Largely opinion, with one vendor case study.

## Key claims

- A language model can write a first draft that an expert edits in a few places, which Morey said is a large productivity gain, even an order of magnitude, and removes the blank page [02:35, 03:05].
- Sherry (AWS) said health and safety excites her most, citing AWS work with the NFL on identifying helmet contact and a "digital athlete" [03:36, 04:08, 04:38].
- A Stats Perform panelist described the sweet spot for AI as assistive tools for domain experts, with an autonomous-driving analogy ("L3" versus "L5") [05:08].
- Sport is its own language: language models state sports facts wrongly with confidence, so they need to be seeded with facts, and tracking data is a visual language that needs its own models [08:42, 09:43, 10:13].
- Morey said new methods allow correlated predictors and even more parameters than observations if variance is controlled (adjusted plus-minus via ridge regression is his example). Random noise inputs still hurt, so an analyst still curates inputs [12:15, 12:47, 13:49, 14:20].
- Liao said more data is not automatically better, since it can be noisy or biased, and models are associational and do not understand objects, so they can fail on oddities [16:23, 16:53, 17:24].
- Morey said that in chess, human-plus-engine teams beat engines only briefly, and any systematic task a human does can eventually be automated; in the short term experts move up a level to curate output [22:26, 22:58, 23:30].
- Sherry said AWS fine-tuned an open-source language model for Fox Sports NFL narratives, using 58,000 statistics, and that language model plus fine-tuning beat training from scratch [25:01, 25:31, 26:01, 26:32].
- A Stats Perform panelist said public match data is only part of the picture; private team data on sleep or personality is not and should not be public, and teams can fuse public and private data [29:07, 29:38, 30:09].
- Liao raised privacy risks if teams require round-the-clock monitoring (sleep, glucose, brain interfaces) and said AI-assisted cheating (staying just under doping thresholds) and deepfakes are coming concerns [31:11, 31:42, 32:13, 32:43, 33:15, 33:45].
- Morey said a deepfake highlight tape could change the case for in-person scouting [35:18].
- Black box: Liao said deep models do not explain their decisions, which matters in a fourth-quarter play call. Sherry replied that production models are fine-tuned against historical outcomes and can reject high-variance recommendations. Liao countered with the tank-and-grass example (a model keyed on grass nearby) [36:20, 38:21, 38:52, 39:23, 40:24].
- A panelist said a coach who relies on a model at a moment of uncertainty is a bad user, and models are assistive tools [41:25].
- Liao said clinicians in a survey said they would gravitate toward the machine in a conflict, and humans may doubt themselves. He said handing over decisions is not yet appropriate [41:56, 42:26, 48:35, 49:06].
- Morey said explainability and predictive power will always be in tension, and gradients can flip because of interactions. Draft model advice is easier to defend when it is simple. His owner example: a late pick was allowed to follow the model because the stake was small [45:01, 45:31, 46:02, 47:05].
- Morey said players are pragmatic: show something useful and they listen. A panelist said weaker players are more open [51:41, 52:11].
- Morey said humans will likely not stay at the top of the stack in most fields, and curating models comes first [55:47, 56:19].
- On existential risk, Liao described the paperclip problem; the Stats Perform panelist was not worried because perception and digitization are unsolved, citing autonomous vehicles [58:54, 1:01:27, 1:03:58, 1:04:29].

## Numbers and definitions

- Talent-visa letter: three pages normally, now a draft edited in three places [02:35].
- "Order of magnitude" productivity gain (speaker's words) [03:05].
- Visual cortex: a panelist said about 50% of the brain is associated with it [10:13].
- Fox Sports fine-tuning: 58,000 statistics and hundreds of parameters [25:31].
- Sherry cited about 60% accuracy training from scratch versus about 80% with a language model plus fine-tuning, and said this figure is from science generally, not sports [26:01, 26:32].
- Fans waiting at concessions: 20 to 25 minutes (Sherry's framing for the walk-out system) [27:04].
- Chess: engines first beat top players in 1996 (caption "'96"); human-plus-engine advantage lasted about four or five years [22:58].
- A coder friend's recursive-to-iterative conversion took 2.5 days and the model did it instantly [57:53, 58:24].
- Midjourney entry won a $100 art prize (caption wording) [59:24].
- Definitions given: symbolic AI (rules), supervised, unsupervised and deep learning (Liao) [14:51, 15:23]; generative AI as predicting the next word [18:25].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fine-tuning a general language model on domain statistics (Fox Sports case) [25:01, 25:31].
- Ridge regression and related regularization for correlated predictors [12:15, 12:47].
- Draft models with year, school and competition proxies, explainable but increasingly complex [44:31, 45:01].
- Contact detection with computer vision for helmet impacts [04:08].
- Public data plus private team data fusion [30:09].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, validation or sample sizes were shown for any sports claim; the Fox Sports result is a vendor's account, and the accuracy figures are not sport-specific.
- Speakers are not labeled in the captions. Attribution above uses context (AWS, Stats Perform, Morey's own roles); some lines (referees, marketing, sleep monitoring, forecasting additions, the 1000-times summarization claim) cannot be assigned with certainty [06:08, 07:12, 07:42, 1:04:59].
- The moderator opens with a joke where one panelist's name is misheard and blamed on hallucination [08:12].
- Panelists contradicted each other on risk and on whether black-box models are manageable [38:52, 40:24, 1:03:58].
- ChatGPT's "neuroball" invention (no concussions, a sport mixing basketball and football) was shown as a creativity example only [19:26].
- Caption problems: "Patrick Lucy", "Sherry"/"Cherry", "Peter" for Patrick, and some garbled lines (for example about explainability and the "tank" story).

## Q&A

- Will catch or touchdown probability stats be available to fans live? Sherry did not know and would follow up [50:41].
- How do you convince athletes ML helps them individually? Morey said players want to improve and listen to useful edges; weaker players are more open [51:41, 52:11].
- Does AI take authenticity out of things such as art? Panelists answered that people want instant, self-serve products, but authenticity is lost when work is synthetic, and sport will stay human [53:13, 54:46].
- Do you take existential concerns seriously? Morey said coders and designers are nervous; Liao described the paperclip problem and enhancement; the Stats Perform panelist was not worried; the close was that worry only seems to go up [57:23, 58:54, 1:03:58, 1:07:32].

FINAL: Caption problems: names garbled (Zarren as "sarin", Evans as "Katherine/Kathy", Lucey as "Lucy", Kuechly, Okereke, Middleton), "200 bips", T1 "about four times three or four times" multiple, and the 0.75 correlation attribution; unlabeled speakers in T2 and T3 attributed from context; the "1000 times" speedup, "50% visual cortex" and Fox accuracy figures are the speakers' own and unverifiable; summary.md not written to disk per instruction.
